title: Six breaths a minute
hookLine: slow breathing around six a minute is linked to calmer heart rhythms in lab studies

lines: IN: A LITTLE FASTER. OUT: A LITTLE SLOWER.
cards: Put two fingers on the inside of your wrist and find your pulse. Breathe in slowly and keep feeling it: usually the beat quickens a little on the way in, and eases off a little on the way out.
It's subtle, and it's normal. Your heart isn't a metronome. It rides your breath like a boat on a swell.

Researchers have studied that rise and fall for a long time, and they keep landing near one pace where it seems to swing widest and smoothest. It's the last day of this week on the science of practice.

teach.b: The rise and fall has a name: respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Arrhythmia sounds alarming, but here it just means healthy variation. Ordinary resting breath is faster.
Slow it to about six a minute, roughly five seconds in and five out, and in lab studies the swings in heart rate tend to grow larger and more regular.
Some researchers call this resonance breathing, because at around that pace the breath and the body's blood pressure reflexes seem to fall into step, the way a push on a swing lands just right.
Now a finding from an unexpected place. In 2001 the British Medical Journal published a small study from Italy.

teach.h: THE ROSARY AND THE MANTRA FOUND IT.
teach.b: Volunteers recited the rosary in Latin, and separately a yoga mantra. Both slowed breathing to close to six breaths a minute, and heart rhythms shifted the same way.

As far as anyone knows, nobody designed either practice with a stopwatch; the pace seems to come from the reciting itself. So what does this week's science let us say? Remember compared to what, and no magic.
These are mostly small lab studies.
Slow breathing is linked to calmer heart rhythms and often to feeling calmer.
It is not a cure, it doesn't prove anything about any faith, and if slowing down ever makes you dizzy or uneasy, yesterday's line holds: it's okay to stop. Look back at the week: Scientia. WEIRD.
Killingsworth. Goyal's review, and what it doesn't show. Lindahl's study.
And now a number you can carry: six.

how: Some people practice slow breathing at around six breaths a minute, often in for about four and out for about six; one small study found the same pace in the rosary and a yoga mantra.

games.q: you try six breaths a minute and start to feel light-headed. what now?
o: go back to your ordinary breath.
games.why: keep it soft, and if it feels wrong, stop. yesterday's line holds: it's okay to stop.

practice: Breathe in through your nose for a slow count of four and out for a slow count of six: ten seconds, six breaths a minute, soft like a long sigh, never forcing your lungs full.
If you lose count, start again at one; if it feels strained, go back to your ordinary breath, and that counts too. Twelve easy breaths, more or less.

wordCard.voice: Resonance breathing, about ten seconds a breath, the pace where heart rhythm tends to swing widest in lab studies.
